h1: Olive Oil Substitute: What to Use Instead, Job by Job
excerpt: The right olive oil substitute depends on what the oil was doing in the dish, so a dressing, a hot pan, a roasting tray and a cake batter each call for a different fat and sometimes a different quantity.
keyTakeaway: There is no single olive oil substitute, because a dressing, a pan, a roasting tray and a cake batter ask the oil for different things. Rice bran and canola cover the hot jobs one for one. Melted butter covers a cake at about a third more volume. A dressing is the one swap that always tastes different.

intro: The pan is hot, the recipe still says olive oil, and the bottle gives up half a teaspoon. What goes in instead depends on what the oil was there to do.
Dressing, frying, roasting and baking are four jobs. Here is the stand-in for each, the ratio wherever it is not one for one, and the flavour you lose.

sections.heading: Match the olive oil substitute to the job

blocks.text: An olive oil substitute is chosen by job, not by bottle. In a dressing the oil is most of the flavour, so any swap changes how the dish tastes. In a hot pan it is mainly a cooking medium and almost any kitchen oil does the work.

sections.heading: Dressings and finishing: the hardest swap

blocks.text: A dressing is oil, acid and salt, so the oil carries most of what the tongue meets. Nothing replaces extra virgin olive oil here without changing the dish. Sunflower and grapeseed come closest in texture, go in one for one, and want extra lemon to stop the result tasting flat.

items: **Sunflower or grapeseed.** Neutral and light, one for one, then sharpen with acid.
**Melted butter.** Fine warm over fish, sets hard as the plate cools.
**Coconut oil.** Only where sweetness belongs; it firms up in a chilled dressing.
**Ghee.** Good through hot rice or dhal, wrong on a cold salad.

blocks.text: Ratios for the real thing are in [extra virgin olive oil salad dressing](/blog/extra-virgin-olive-oil-salad-dressing).

Home tumis runs roughly 140-180°C and most kitchen oils handle it without complaint. Rice bran and canola swap in one for one and add nothing to the flavour, which in a heavily spiced dish is the point. Ghee goes in one for one and brings a nutty dairy note.
Butter alone scorches at tumis heat because of the milk solids in it. Use it half and half with a neutral oil, or use ghee instead.

Roasting asks a fat to coat, brown and stay put for half an hour at 180-200°C. Rice bran, canola and melted ghee all do that one for one. Coconut oil roasts cleanly too, though it leaves a sweetness better suited to pumpkin than to rosemary potatoes.

items: **Rice bran or canola.** One for one, neutral, cheapest by the litre.
**Melted ghee.** One for one, deeper browning, a dairy smell in the oven.
**Coconut oil.** One for one, measured melted, sweet on root vegetables.
**Butter.** Toss it through at the end of the roast, not the start.

sections.heading: Baking, and the one ratio worth remembering

blocks.text: A cake built on olive oil wants a liquid fat, and melted butter is the usual stand-in. Butter carries water as well as fat, so use about a third more by weight: 100 ml of olive oil becomes roughly 135 g of melted butter, cooled first.
Coconut oil bakes well in anything already sweet, one for one and measured melted. Ghee suits a dense bake and reads as dairy.

sections.heading: When olive oil is the substitute

blocks.text: Olive oil stands in for other fats as often as the reverse. It replaces butter or margarine in many bakes at roughly three-quarters the volume, and it replaces a neutral oil one for one in dressings, marinades and gentle pan work. The dish gains a peppery edge.

items: **For butter in a cake.** Three-quarters the volume, and a mild oil rather than a bitter one.
**For a neutral oil in the pan.** One for one, under the [olive oil smoke point](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take).
**For a neutral oil in a marinade.** One for one, then taste before adding acid.
**Not for the deep fryer.** Frying oil is not reused, and a full pot is expensive.

Ask what the oil was doing. In a dressing nothing swaps cleanly, so add acid and accept a different salad. In a pan, rice bran or canola. In a cake, melted butter.

faqs.q: What can I use instead of olive oil?
faqs.a: Rice bran, canola or sunflower oil cover frying and roasting one for one. Melted butter or ghee cover baking and finishing. A dressing has no clean swap, so use a neutral oil and more acid.

faqs.q: What is the best olive oil substitute for baking?
faqs.a: Melted butter, at about a third more volume than the oil, because butter carries water as well as fat. A neutral oil such as canola goes in one for one and tastes plainer.

faqs.q: Can I use butter instead of olive oil for frying?
faqs.a: Not on its own at tumis heat, because the milk solids in butter scorch before the food is done. Use half butter and half neutral oil, or use ghee, which has those solids removed.

faqs.q: Is coconut oil a good substitute for olive oil?
faqs.a: In curries, rendang and sweet bakes, yes, one for one and measured melted. In a salad dressing it brings a sweet coconut note that most of those dishes were not built around.

faqs.q: How much olive oil replaces butter in a recipe?
faqs.a: Roughly three-quarters the volume of butter called for, since olive oil is fat all the way through. A hundred grams of butter becomes about 75 ml of oil in most cake batters.

faqs.q: What can I use instead of olive oil in a salad dressing?
faqs.a: Sunflower or grapeseed oil one for one, with a little more lemon juice or vinegar to keep the dressing from tasting flat. Melted butter works warm over vegetables but sets firm.
